x: The EU regulation timeline is a private spare-time project by Steffen Zimmermann. It follows the EU's digital and product legislation (the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS-2, the AI Act, the Machinery Regulation, the European Product Act and the acts around them) from the official sources, and turns them into a timeline, procedure pages, standards overviews and a forecast of when open procedures are likely to become law. It is independent: it does not speak for any employer, association or institution, and it is not legal advice. The legal texts on EUR-Lex prevail. Using the graphics and texts Everything here may be copied, shared and adapted, also commercially, under CC BY 4.0 . Please name the source like this: Steffen Zimmermann, git-z0man.github.io/eu-regulation-timeline, CC BY 4.0 Copy Every graphic carries this line at its bottom, and its SVG file the same information as metadata. Please keep it when you reuse a graphic, and say if you changed it.

The site is built and kept up to date with the help of an AI model (Claude, by Anthropic): routines read the official sources every day, analyse new documents and publish the site, and working sessions build and change it. x: Regulations › Authorities › ECCC as of 5 Nov 2026 The EU body that funds cybersecurity, set up in 2021 in Bucharest with the Network of National Coordination Centres. It implements the cybersecurity parts of the Digital Europe Programme, whose work programme it adopts, and of Horizon Europe, and the funding actions of the Cyber Solidarity Act (Cyber Hubs, preparedness, mutual assistance). Financially autonomous since September 2024; its mandate ends on 31 December 2029 unless it is extended. Seat: Bucharest (Romania) Mandate: Art. 3-10 and 21 ECCC Regulation; until 31 Dec 2029 (Art. 47) ECCC website In 2025 EUR 238.3 million committed, EUR 182.0 million paid 69% of the payment appropriations were used; at the end of the year EUR 495.7 million were promised to projects and not yet paid, up from EUR 442.7 million a year before. Regulations › Authorities › ENISA as of 5 Nov 2026 The EU's agency for cybersecurity, set up in 2004 and given a permanent mandate by the Cybersecurity Act in 2019. It supports the Member States and the EU institutions in implementing NIS-2, the Cyber Resilience Act and the Cyber Solidarity Act, prepares the European cybersecurity certification schemes and runs the EU vulnerability database and the CRA single reporting platform. The Commission's proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 would replace its mandate. Seat: Athens (Greece), with an office in Heraklion and a local office in Brussels Mandate: Art. 3-12 and 19-45 CSA Pending: Cybersecurity Act 2 ENISA website In 2025 EUR 55.0 million, 51% of it from the Commission Union contribution EUR 26.7 million; agreements with the Commission for agreed actions EUR 28.1 million; of the money for those actions available in 2025, 15% was paid out by the end of the year. x: Analysis · 14 Nov 2026 Where ENISA consults: ten channels, two feeds, and drafts that are announced elsewhere ENISA does not publish more than it did in 2023, but in more places and by more rules. Its certification work consults in an orderly way on its own website. Its guidance for manufacturers under the Cyber Resilience Act was put out for comment in 2026 as PDF files on its server, mostly without a news item on its site, and became known through LinkedIn and community mailing lists. The Cybersecurity Act 2 would make such guidance a standing task of ENISA, so far without a duty to consult on it. (also in German: Wo ENISA konsultiert: zehn Kanäle, zwei Feeds und Entwürfe, die anderswo angekündigt werden) Analysis · 5 Nov 2026 Is ENISA equipped for its tasks? Half its money is temporary, and the Cybersecurity Act 2 would mainly make it permanent ENISA's own budget has grown little since 2022 while the acts giving it tasks multiplied. The growth came from time-limited agreements with the Commission: in 2025 they paid 51 % of its revenue, and they run out in 2028. The Commission's proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 would turn much of that money into a permanent budget, but adds little on top, and its timing, the next EU budget and the fees are open. (also in German: Ist ENISA für ihre Aufgaben gerüstet? Die Hälfte ihres Geldes ist befristet, und der Cybersecurity Act 2 würde es vor allem verstetigen)

Date Document Issuer Status Read (rendered) 24 Jul 2026 Draft candidate EUMSS Scheme v1.1 for Public Review Our summary: ENISA's draft candidate European cybersecurity certification scheme for managed security services (EUMSS), version 1.1 of July 2026, prepared under the Cybersecurity Act at the Commission's request with ENISA's ad hoc working group and published for public review; it is a draft, not adopted and not law. It certifies one service, not the provider: in this first version only incident response, against a common horizontal layer of baseline requirements (an ISMS under ISO/IEC 27001 or an equivalent standard, supplier control, SBOMs, vulnerability management) plus service-specific requirements, at assurance level basic, substantial or high, always by an accredited conformity assessment body and never by self-assessment. Certificates are valid for at most three years with annual surveillance, and substantial and high require evidence that the controls have operated for 6 or 12 months. Several parts are still open, among them the transition period for national schemes (12 or 24 months), recognition agreements with third countries and the terminology annex. Proposal: 19 Nov 2025 · Adopted: 8 Jul 2026 · Published: 24 Jul 2026 What it changes in AI Act: Amends the AI Act in 43 points to simplify its implementation; among others it replaces Art. 4 (AI literacy), moves the obligations for high-risk AI systems to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I) (Art. 113 as amended) and gives providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026 to comply with Art. 50(2) (Art. 111(4)). What it changes in MR: Empowers the Commission to add health and safety requirements for AI systems that are high-risk under Art. 6(1) AI Act to Annex III of the Machinery Regulation by delegated act, applying by 2 August 2028 (Art. 8 and 47 amended), and adds a transitional rule on the harmonised standards and common specifications of the AI Act for such systems (new Art. 20(10)).

Januar 2024, BAnz AT 02.02.2024 B1 · status on its page: “Einreichung möglich” Funds companies taking part in national, European and international standardisation committees (DIN/DKE, CEN/CENELEC, ETSI, ISO/IEC), where the harmonised standards under these acts are written. 3.1 Standardisation – companies: Active work in up to two standardisation committees at a time not joined in the last three years (also through a mandated third party); flat rates per meeting (European: 1,500 EUR in person, 750 EUR virtual), standards management, a DIN SPEC or VDE SPEC. Up to 45,000 EUR, 70 % of the expenses, up to 36 months. Who: Companies with up to 1,000 staff and 100 million EUR turnover, with a site in Germany; de minimis. Applications until 31 May 2027. 3.2 Knowledge transfer through standardisation: Preparing research results for standardisation, R&D on digital standardisation; at least one standardisation proposal. Up to 200,000 EUR per partner; companies usually up to 50 %, SMEs up to 80 %, research up to 85 %. Who: Consortia of companies, standards bodies and their committees, universities and research organisations in Germany. Sketches until 31 May 2026 (passed), applications until 31 May 2027. 2.1 Patenting – companies: A first patent application. Up to 50 %; module 1 up to 10,000

public statements of the last 12 months 11 Nov 2026 · Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy European Parliament, plenary · Resilience against cyber and other hybrid attacks, protecting critical infrastructure and essential supply chains · spoke 2 times Our summary: Virkkunen closes the plenary debate on resilience against cyber and other hybrid attacks and the protection of critical infrastructure. She says the debate showed that sound rules are not enough and that stronger capabilities, secure technologies, trusted suppliers and European cooperation are needed. The Commission will reduce strategic weaknesses and strengthen cyber-preparedness, and she asks Parliament to work with it; no new act or date is named. not only sound rules, but also stronger capabilities, secure technologies, trusted suppliers and effective European cooperation – Henna Virkkunen, original language (EN) Our summary: Virkkunen opens the debate on resilience against cyber and hybrid attacks. After incidents that switched off refrigeration systems in supermarkets and blood banks, she puts supply chain security at the core of the Cybersecurity Act revision, asks for clear timelines to phase high-risk suppliers out of 5G networks before 6G, for a stronger ENISA, and for full implementation of the CRA and NIS2. supply chain security is at the core of the proposal for the revision of the Cybersecurity Act, which is now on the table in this House. – Henna

Regulations › Topics of high interest "High-risk supplier" is on its way to becoming a horizontal eligibility filter in EU law: it would decide who may supply key ICT assets of essential and important entities, take part in public procurement and auctions, receive public support and EU funding, and take part in European standardisation, certification and conformity assessment. No act in force defines the term. The only definition is in the Commission proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 (Art. 2(39)); the proposals for an Industrial Accelerator Act and a Public Procurement Act already refer to it. The law in force works one step earlier, with non-technical risk factors (NIS-2, Cyber Resilience Act) and third-country jurisdiction tests in renewable energy auctions (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1176). Our own assessment as of 26 Nov 2026; not legal advice. Only the law in force is binding. Proposals and negotiation drafts are not law and can still change; a draft report or a compromise text is the position of one rapporteur or Presidency, not of the institution. t: New Standardisation Regulation – routes to presumption of conformity
x: Regulations › Topics of high interest On 6 October 2026 the Commission proposed a new Standardisation Regulation (COM(2026) 780) to replace Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012. It keeps CEN, CENELEC and ETSI at the centre but adds routes to a presumption of conformity when they cannot deliver in time: harmonised standardisation deliverables as an interim step, standards from designated standards development organisations, and a horizontal power to adopt common specifications. Requests get fixed content (a deadline per standard and an expiry date), the European standardisation organisations get performance indicators, and every referenced standard becomes free to read online. The Regulation would apply six months after entry into force, expected in 2028, without transitional rules. Acts such as the CRA and the Machinery Regulation tie their presumption to harmonised standards under Regulation 1025/2012; the proposal redirects those references but does not amend them. A draft, not law. Our own assessment as of 11 Oct 2026; not legal advice. Only the law in force is binding. Proposals and negotiation drafts are not law and can still change; a draft report or a compromise text is the position of one rapporteur or Presidency, not of the institution. t: Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) für den Maschinenbau
x: Frage Antwort Fällt Ihre Maschine unter den CRA?¹ Ja, wenn sie Software oder programmierbare Elektronik enthält und sich mit einem Gerät oder Netz verbinden kann, auch über Kabel, Service-Schnittstelle oder Fernwartung. Ohne jede Datenverbindung nicht. Gilt dann die Maschinenverordnung nicht mehr?² Doch. Beide gelten nebeneinander: zwei Bewertungen, eine gemeinsame Konformitätserklärung. Wer den CRA erfüllt, erfüllt Teile der Maschinenverordnung zur Korrumpierung leichter, nicht automatisch. Welche Stücke sind betroffen?³ Jedes Stück, das ab 11.12.2027 in Verkehr kommt, auch aus laufender Serie. Ältere Stücke nur, wenn sie ab dann wesentlich geändert werden. h: Beispiel: Ausgenutzte Lücke in einer zugekauften Steuerung
x: Schritt Was passiert Ausgangslage¹ Ihre Verpackungsmaschine, 2025 ausgeliefert, enthält eine zugekaufte Steuerung mit Weboberfläche und Fernwartung. Die Maschine fällt unter die Meldepflicht des CRA. Tag 0² Der Steuerungshersteller warnt: Eine Lücke seiner Steuerung wird bereits ausgenutzt. Melden muss das er, für seine Steuerung. Sie melden nur, was in einer Ihrer Maschinen ausgenutzt wird. Sofort prüfen³ Ist die Weboberfläche in Ihren Maschinen aktiv und von außen erreichbar? Melden Kunden Auffälligkeiten? Warnen Sie die Kunden, auch wenn der CRA das hier noch nicht verlangt: Weboberfläche abschalten, Fernzugang trennen. Angriff bei Ihrem Kunden⁴ Ein Kunde meldet einen Einbruch über die Weboberfläche. Nach Ihrer ersten Prüfung sind Sie hinreichend sicher: Die Lücke ist in einer Ihrer Maschinen ausgenutzt. Ab jetzt laufen 24 Stunden für die Frühwarnung und 72 für die Meldung an das koordinierende CSIRT, bei Hauptniederlassung in Deutschland das BSI; die betroffenen Kunden informieren Sie. Nach dem Update⁵ Binnen 14 Tagen, nachdem eine Behebung oder Abhilfe verfügbar ist, folgt Ihr Abschlussbericht. Schon das Abschalten der Weboberfläche kann eine solche Abhilfe sein. Ab 11.12.2027⁶ Für neue Stücke müssen Sie Updates dann kostenlos liefern, Schwachstellen nach Anhang I Teil II behandeln und die Steuerung in der Stückliste führen. x: Gilt ein Umbau beim Kunden als Bereitstellen? Davon hängt ab, ob Sie für eine fremde Maschine Hersteller werden und ob Ihre eigene ältere Maschine danach den CRA erfüllen muss. Kein Text sagt es. Die Leitlinien der Kommission (C/2026/6013, unverbindlich, Rn. 116 und 117) machen erst das Bereitstellen der geänderten Maschine zu einem neuen Inverkehrbringen, beantworten die Frage aber nicht. Wie lang muss der Unterstützungszeitraum bei Maschinen sein, die 15 bis 20 Jahre laufen? Der Text verlangt die erwartete Nutzungsdauer und mindestens fünf Jahre; eine Obergrenze nennt er nicht. Ist ein nie geändertes Standardpasswort eine Schwachstelle, deren Ausnutzung Sie melden müssen? Text und Leitlinien sagen es nicht ausdrücklich. Nach unserer Lesart ist die Begriffsbestimmung weit genug. Auch Hersteller selbst sehen es so: Ein Hersteller von Steuerungen für Kälteanlagen hat im November 2026 die im Handbuch dokumentierten Standardpasswörter seiner Altgeräte selbst als Schwachstelle veröffentlicht (CVE-2026-127057). t: Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) für den Maschinenbau
x: Was Inhalt Frage an Lieferanten¹ Bringen Sie die Komponente selbst in Verkehr, mit CE nach CRA ab 11.12.2027? Bis wann liefern Sie Sicherheitsupdates? Wie melden Sie uns Schwachstellen? Stückliste² Fragen Sie nach der Software-Stückliste der Komponente. Das ist eine Bitte: Der CRA verpflichtet den Lieferanten nicht dazu, er kann ablehnen. In Ihrer eigenen Stückliste führen Sie mindestens die Komponente selbst als oberste Abhängigkeit; Schwachstellen darin behandeln Sie trotzdem. Supportende abgleichen³ Bei der Festlegung Ihres Supportendes dürfen Sie den Support der Steuerung berücksichtigen; Ihre Pflicht endet damit nicht. Wählen Sie Komponenten, deren Unterstützung so lange läuft wie Ihre. Lieferant ohne Sitz in der EU⁴ Kaufen Sie direkt beim Hersteller außerhalb der EU, klären Sie, wer die Komponente einführt. Führen Sie selbst ein, können Sie Einführerpflichten treffen; für Ihre Maschine bleiben Sie ohnehin Hersteller. Herkunft⁵ Der CRA fragt nicht nach dem Herkunftsland. Er verlangt Sicherheit, Support und Updates; nicht technische Risiken, etwa aus Drittstaaten, berücksichtigt die Marktüberwachung. Ersatzteile⁶ Identische Ersatzteile fallen nicht unter den CRA, wenn Sie sie gezielt zur Reparatur liefern, etwa über den Service mit Angabe der Maschine. Identisch heißt: gleiche Funktion und gleiche sicherheitsrelevante Eigenschaften. Ein Teil mit neuerem Chip oder neuer Firmware kann identisch sein, solange Protokolle, Kryptografie und Zugangsschutz gleich bleiben.

t: Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) für den Maschinenbau
x: Produkt mit digitalen Elementen Hard- oder Software samt der dazugehörigen Datenverarbeitung aus der Ferne, auch einzeln verkaufte Komponenten. Unter den CRA fällt es, wenn es sich mit einem Gerät oder Netz verbinden kann. Inverkehrbringen Die erste Bereitstellung auf dem EU-Markt. Bei Maschinen und anderer Hardware zählt jedes einzelne Stück, nicht der Typ. Bei Software, die Sie eigenständig anbieten, zählt die Version: Alle Kopien einer Version gelten mit dem ersten Angebot als in Verkehr gebracht (Leitlinien der Kommission). Wesentliche Änderung Eine Änderung nach dem Inverkehrbringen, die sich auf die Erfüllung des Anhangs I Teil I auswirkt oder den bewerteten Zweck ändert. Nicht dasselbe wie die wesentliche Veränderung der Maschinenverordnung. Aktiv ausgenutzte Schwachstelle Eine Schwachstelle, bei der es verlässliche Belege gibt, dass ein Angreifer sie ohne Zustimmung des Systemeigners ausgenutzt hat. Melden müssen Sie sie, wenn sie in Ihrer Maschine steckt und in einer Ihrer Maschinen ausgenutzt wurde, nicht schon, wenn sie anderswo ausgenutzt wird (so die Leitlinien der Kommission). Unterstützungszeitraum Die Zeit, in der Sie Schwachstellen beheben und Sicherheitsupdates liefern: so lange, wie die Maschine voraussichtlich genutzt wird, mindestens fünf Jahre. Software-Stückliste (SBOM) Maschinenlesbare Liste der Software-Bestandteile Ihres Produkts, mindestens der obersten Abhängigkeiten. Produkt-Cybersicherheit Wer im Unternehmen Schwachstellen, Updates und Meldungen

Frage Antwort Gelten die Regeln zur Lieferkette auch für Ihre Firma?¹ Ja, nach dem Vorschlag fällt jeder Maschinenbauer darunter, auch kleine. Pflichten entstehen erst durch Beschlüsse der Kommission, die sie auf größere Firmen begrenzen kann. Was in Ihrem Werk kann es treffen?² Teile von Hochrisikoanbietern, vor allem in Anlagen, die die Kommission als besonders kritisch einstuft. Betrifft es die Maschinen, die Sie liefern?³ Nur wenn Elektronik oder Software eines Hochrisikoanbieters darin steckt. Ein Verbot träfe dann Ihren Kunden. Kann ein Lieferant oder Ihre Firma Hochrisikoanbieter sein, auch mit Sitz in der EU?⁴ Ja, wenn sie aus einem Drittland gesteuert wird und die Kommission dieses Land, die Firma oder ihren Mutterkonzern benennt. Betrifft es Ihre Kunden?⁵ Ja. Kunden in Energie, Verkehr, Wasser, Chemie, Pharma, Lebensmitteln und Fahrzeugbau fallen ab 50 Beschäftigten unter NIS-2, unter den Vorschlag auch kleinere. Der Berichtsentwurf will, dass sie Zertifiziertes kaufen. Gibt es schon eine Liste der Produkte, die betroffen sein können?⁶ Im Vorschlag und beim Ratsvorsitz nur Telekommunikationsnetze. Der Berichtsentwurf nimmt etwa Windräder samt Steuerung auf; für Funkmodule soll die Kommission binnen zwölf Monaten mit der Prüfung beginnen. Nichts davon ist Recht. x: Schritt Was passiert Heute¹ Ihre Anlage beim Lebensmittelhersteller hat ein Gateway eines Anbieters mit Mutterkonzern im Drittland. Nichts ist verboten. Wann? Heute. CSA2 gilt² Die Behörde kann vom Kunden Lieferanten und Aufbau der Anlage verlangen; der Kunde fragt Sie nach Herkunft und Fernzugriff. Wann? Nach unserer Schätzung ab 2028. Risikobewertung³ Drei Mitgliedstaaten oder die Kommission beantragen eine Bewertung, etwa der Fernwartung in der Produktion. Wann? Nach unserer Schätzung eher 2029, bei frühem Gesetz schon 2028. Durchführungsrechtsakte⁴ Die Kommission benennt das Drittland, ermittelt solche Gateways als wichtige IKT-Assets und verbietet Hochrisiko-Teile darin. Wann? Nach unserer Schätzung 2029 bis 2030. Liste und Auslauf⁵ Die Liste nennt den Anbieter. Bis zum Ende der Auslauffrist muss der Kunde das Gateway ersetzen; wer zahlt, regelt der Vorschlag nicht. Wann? Nach unserer Schätzung nach 2030. Was Sie jetzt tun⁶ Sie regeln in neuen Kundenverträgen, wer einen verlangten Austausch zahlt, und planen für neue Anlagen ein Gateway mit Ersatzlieferant. Wann? Jetzt. Gilt der Teil zur Lieferkette auch unterhalb der NIS-2-Größenschwelle? Nach dem Wortlaut ja; ein Durchführungsrechtsakt kann ihn nach Größe begrenzen. Wird Hochrisikoanbieter, wer aus einem benannten Land kommt, oder nur, wer einzeln geprüft wurde? Der Rat hat den Text des Vorsitzes dazu nur teilweise freigegeben. Frage Antwort Für welche Ihrer Produkte gilt die MVO?¹ Für Maschinen, unvollständige Maschinen und dazugehörige Produkte wie Sicherheitsbauteile, die Sie ab 20.1.2027 in Verkehr bringen oder für den eigenen Betrieb bauen und in Betrieb nehmen. Was ist mit Maschinen, die schon beim Kunden stehen?² Sie bleiben, wie sie sind. Wer eine solche Maschine später wesentlich verändert, wird für sie Hersteller nach der MVO, auch der Betreiber selbst; ausgenommen ist nur, wer nicht beruflich handelt und für den Eigengebrauch umbaut. Brauchen Sie künftig eine Prüfstelle?³ Nur für Anhang I: Teil A immer, Teil B nur ohne passende harmonisierte Norm. In Teil A stehen auch Sicherheitsbauteile und eingebettete Systeme mit selbstlernendem Verhalten für Sicherheitsfunktionen. Welche Anforderungen sind neu?⁴ Vor allem: Schutz gegen Manipulation über Verbindungen, Steuerungen, die vorhersehbaren Angriffen standhalten, soweit es das Risiko verlangt, Protokolle von Eingriffen und Software-Versionen, Regeln für lernende Steuerungen. Gilt daneben der Cyber Resilience Act?⁵ Ja, wenn Ihre Maschine Software hat und sich mit einem Gerät oder Netz verbinden kann: Meldepflicht schon heute, alles Übrige ab 11.12.2027. Beide Bewertungen, eine Konformitätserklärung. Was gilt für Anlagen aus mehreren Maschinen?⁶ Eine verkettete Anlage, die als Ganzes gesteuert wird, ist selbst eine Maschine. Wer sie zusammenstellt und in Verkehr bringt oder in Betrieb nimmt, ist ihr Hersteller. Fundstellen: ¹ abgeleitet: Art.

t: NIS-2 und BSIG für den Maschinenbau
x: Frage Antwort Fällt Ihr Unternehmen unter NIS-2?¹ Ja, wenn Sie Maschinen herstellen und mindestens 50 Beschäftigte oder je über 10 Mio. € Umsatz und Bilanzsumme haben. Dann sind Sie wichtige Einrichtung. Zählen Mutter- und Schwesterunternehmen mit?² In der Regel ja. Beschäftigte und Umsatz verbundener Unternehmen zählen mit, von Partnerunternehmen anteilig, außer Ihre IT ist von ihnen unabhängig. Was gilt für Anlagenbau, Montage und Service?³ Erfasst ist, wer Maschinen herstellt; vernachlässigbare Nebentätigkeiten können außer Betracht bleiben. Wer nur montiert oder repariert, steht nicht in den Anlagen, außer über eine andere Tätigkeit. Gilt NIS-2 auch für die Maschinen, die Sie liefern?⁴ Nein, NIS-2 betrifft die IT und OT Ihres eigenen Betriebs. Für Ihre Maschinen gilt der CRA, voll ab 11.12.2027. Kunden in NIS-2-Sektoren müssen aber ihre Lieferkette absichern und fragen deshalb Sie. Welche Kunden sind das?⁵ Ab mittlerer Größe Kunden aus Energie, Verkehr, Wasser, Gesundheit und Pharma, Abfall, Chemie, Lebensmittelindustrie und dem verarbeitenden Gewerbe von Elektronik bis Fahrzeugbau. Sie haben sich noch nicht registriert?⁶ Holen Sie es sofort nach. Die Frist für Unternehmen, die seit 6.12.2025 erfasst sind, lief Anfang März 2026 ab. Das BSI kann selbst registrieren und ein Bußgeld verhängen. Prüfen Sie heute, ob Sie beim BSI registriert sind, und setzen Sie die Risikomaßnahmen für Ihre IT und OT um.¹ NIS-2 regelt Ihren Betrieb, nicht Ihre Maschinen; für die gilt der CRA, voll ab 11.12.2027. Das BSI prüft wichtige Einrichtungen, wenn Tatsachen auf Mängel deuten. Ihre Maßnahmen müssen Sie dokumentieren, regelmäßig vorlegen nicht.² Ein Vorschlag der Kommission stellt Leitlinien für Fragebögen an Lieferanten in Aussicht, ein anderer würde eine CRA-Meldung eines schweren Produktvorfalls, die die nötigen Angaben enthält, auch als NIS-2-Meldung zählen lassen. If it held, one could look much further back and say more about whether legal acts are becoming more complex ( section 7 ). From this grew a broader search. Besides the three criteria came the gaps the forecast names itself and further candidates: “Have your say” (consultations, number of responses), recitals, committees and political groups, the State of the Union address, reports such as the Draghi report, and crises. Kurz nach der Veröffentlichung am 10. Oktober 2026 kam die Rückmeldung eines Experten des VDMA, des Verbands des Maschinen- und Anlagenbaus, der sich mit dem European Product Act befasst. x: The Commission's timetables for new laws are often tight. The forecast sets against them how long comparable procedures really took. The technical term is reference class forecasting: instead of estimating from one's own plan, one looks at how long all comparable cases took. The reference class: 1,016 files of the ordinary legislative procedure since 2012 that were negotiated or are still open. Negotiated means: with trilogues, at second reading, or at first reading with more than 60 days between the votes in committee and in plenary, without codifications and urgent procedures ( section 7 ). For each open file only the comparable files count that had reached the same step and had not moved on after as long a wait; since 13 October 2026 only the 40 % nearest to it in size. 4,000 runs per law give the median and the range. Parliament's breaks around the European elections are taken out, and the break of 2029 is put in. Self-test. The forecast was tested on all 427 proposals of 2016–2021, each from the day of its proposal and with only what was known then. The real date fell in the middle half for 48.5 % of them (target 50 %) and in the range of eight in ten runs for 81.0 % (target 80 %). For the typical file the median missed by 6.9 months. The forecast knows where a file stands and what the calendar looks like. h: Rule of thumb: does size work linearly?
x: In quarters one sees a staircase; the question is whether it keeps rising evenly. In tenths the median for words of legal text rises from 11.3 months in the smallest tenth to 29.4 in the largest. That is not linear in the number of words: from the fifth to the tenth tenth the typical text grows 6.7 times, the duration only by 69 %. It is linear in the logarithm of the words. Each doubling of the legal text lengthens the procedure in the median by about 16 %, ten times as much text by about 64 %. The chart shows it: the ten medians lie on one curve within their uncertainty. t: How the forecast was built Wie der Forecast entstanden ist
x: Data. For each of the 1,354 files since 2012 three sources were read. The file's page in Parliament's Legislative Observatory gives the committees, rapporteur, political group, priority lists, urgency and the opinions of national parliaments. The text of the Commission proposal in EUR-Lex gives recitals, articles, words and commas, measured the same way for every year. The “Have your say” portal gives consultations and responses. Dated events were added, each with its source: State of the Union addresses, the Joint Declarations on legislative priorities, the pandemic, the invasion of Ukraine, the Letta and Draghi reports. Three tests per candidate. First, the comparison of medians: how long did files in the smallest and in the largest quarter take? Second, the speed factor from a survival model (Cox): above 1 means faster, below 1 slower, adjusted for the election calendar and for whether a proposal amends existing acts. Third, the test on later, unseen files: a model built on the proposals of 2012–2017, applied to those of 2018–2022. Only this third test shows whether a candidate makes a forecast better. t: Where ENISA consults: ten channels, two feeds, and drafts that are announced elsewhere
x: English Deutsch Regulation Desk › Analysis ENISA does not publish more than it did in 2023, but in more places and by more rules. Its certification work consults in an orderly way on its own website. Its guidance for manufacturers under the Cyber Resilience Act was put out for comment in 2026 as PDF files on its server, mostly without a news item on its site, and became known through LinkedIn and community mailing lists. The Cybersecurity Act 2 would make such guidance a standing task of ENISA, so far without a duty to consult on it. 14 Nov 2026 The question ENISA writes more and more documents that manufacturers and software developers are expected to use: technical advisories on the Cyber Resilience Act, guidance on NIS-2 and certification schemes. Many go out as drafts for comment first. How does someone without a seat in an ENISA or Commission group learn that a draft is open, and by when they can comment? We checked ENISA's websites and its consultations from 2023 to November 2026. In brief More places, not more documents. ENISA's publication list counts 34 items for 2023, 24 for 2024, 20 for 2025 and 22 up to 14 November 2026. What grew is the number of channels. Two of ten channels offer an RSS feed, and GitHub can be watched. The main website has had no RSS since its relaunch at the end of 2024, and there is no page listing open consultations and surveys. Certification consults in an orderly way, on its own website, for four to ten weeks. Guidance for manufacturers

t: Is ENISA equipped for its tasks? Half its money is temporary, and the Cybersecurity Act 2 would mainly make it permanent
x: English Deutsch Regulation Desk › Analysis ENISA's own budget has grown little since 2022 while the acts giving it tasks multiplied. The growth came from time-limited agreements with the Commission: in 2025 they paid 51 % of its revenue, and they run out in 2028. The Commission's proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 would turn much of that money into a permanent budget, but adds little on top, and its timing, the next EU budget and the fees are open. 5 Nov 2026 The question Is the EU Agency for Cybersecurity equipped, in money and staff, for the tasks the acts give it now and will give it? We read its annual accounts from 2019 to 2025, its programming document for 2026 to 2028, the financial statement of the Commission's proposal for a Cybersecurity Act 2 and the negotiating texts published so far. The figures and charts are on the new ENISA page . Two kinds of money ENISA has two sources of money. The first is the Union contribution, which the budgetary authority sets each year. It rose from EUR 16.3 million in 2019 to EUR 24.2 million in 2022, with the permanent mandate of the Cybersecurity Act, and then more slowly, to EUR 26.7 million in 2025 (EEA and EFTA states included). The programming document plans EUR 27.9 million for 2028. The second is money the Commission gives ENISA for actions agreed with it, mostly from the Digital Europe Programme: EUR 15 million in 2023 for the pilot of the Cybersecurity Support Action, EUR 16 million in 2024 and EUR 28.1 million in 2025. t: How our forecast is made, and how to read it
x: English Deutsch Regulation Desk › Analysis When will a law that is still being negotiated be in the Official Journal? Our forecast answers with what comparable EU laws actually took, not with plans. This memo explains where it comes from, how it works, how often it was right in the past and what it cannot know. 14 Oct 2026 The question Companies, associations and authorities plan around EU laws that are not adopted yet: when to build up compliance, when to give input, when the standards will be needed. The Commission's own planning is one answer, but it is a plan. Our forecast gives a second one: how long laws like this one took in the past, from the point it has reached today. The idea: compare with what really happened The method is called reference class forecasting. Instead of estimating a duration from a plan, it looks at a class of comparable cases and how long they really took. For EU laws, these cases are well documented: the European Parliament's Legislative Observatory lists the key events of every file of the ordinary legislative procedure. What goes into it Comparable laws. All 1,005 files of the ordinary legislative procedure proposed since 2012 that were negotiated in trilogues. Files that were withdrawn or adopted without negotiations are left out. The Legislative Observatory recorded trilogues reliably only from about 2015, so an earlier first reading counts as negotiated when Parliament voted more than 60 days after its committee. t: Large laws take longer: our forecast now compares like with like
x: English Deutsch Regulation Desk › Analysis We tested which properties of a proposal go with how long the EU takes to adopt it. Size wins clearly; commas, consultations and the State of the Union address do not. Since 13 October the forecast compares each file with files of similar size, and most dates move later. 13 Oct 2026 Where we started On 10 October we published a forecast of when the open EU legislative procedures we follow are likely to reach the Official Journal. It compares each file with every file of the ordinary legislative procedure since 2012 that was negotiated in trilogues, from the step the file has reached. It also said what it did not know: political priority, the size of a file, deals between the institutions and crises. An expert's question An expert of VDMA, the German mechanical engineering industry association, suggested looking at complexity: the number of articles, the amount of legal text, the number of commas or commas per article. The hunch was that this would give a better model than looking at the past alone. The second question was whether proposals are becoming more complex. What we measured For all 1,347 files of the ordinary legislative procedure since 2012 in the European Parliament's Legislative Observatory, we measured the English text of the Commission proposal in the same way for every year: recitals, articles and annexes, words and commas. 1,288 of 1,330 proposals could be measured. t: The forecast for statisticians: estimand, algorithm, evaluation and limits
x: English Deutsch Regulation Desk › Analysis A technical note on our forecast of EU legislative procedures: a conditional, non-parametric reference class forecast with a size neighbourhood and a calendar transformation. Evaluated out of sample with PIT, interval coverage and the CRPS, including a check for look-ahead in our own backtest. What holds up, what does not, and where we would welcome advice. 14 Oct 2026 Summary For each open file of the ordinary legislative procedure (COD) that we follow, we forecast the date of publication in the Official Journal. The forecast resamples the trajectories of comparable past files: files that reached the same step, had not moved on after the same elapsed working time, and are close in size, measured as words of legal text of the Commission proposal. Out of sample (426 files proposed 2016–2021, each forecast on the day of its proposal), the size neighbourhood lowers the mean CRPS from 7.75 to 7.14 months (paired bootstrap interval of the difference −0.79 to −0.42). The central intervals are close to nominal at every level: the 50 % interval covers 49 %, the 80 % interval 81 %, the 90 % interval 88 %. Two corrections of 14 October 2026 got us there: a definition of the reference class that no longer loses negotiated files of 2012–2014, and a fallback that never drops the condition on the time a file has waited. x: English Deutsch Regulation Desk › Analysis Harmonised standards cited in the Official Journal can be read free of charge on the portals of the national standardisation bodies; drafts only during the public enquiry. A country-by-country list, what it means for the Cyber Resilience Act standards, and what the proposed new Standardisation Regulation would change. 24 Nov 2026 In short Published and cited harmonised standards of CEN and CENELEC: free to read on the read-only portal of a national standardisation body, mostly after a free registration. Some give a PDF (Czech Republic, Slovakia, DKE in Germany). ETSI standards: free anyway, on the ETSI website. Drafts of CEN and CENELEC: free only during the public enquiry, on the national commenting portals; comments go through the national body. A European standard that is not cited in the Official Journal is not on the portals and is sold. EN 40000-1-1:2026 and EN 40000-1-2:2026 for the Cyber Resilience Act, published on 18 November 2026, are such cases: their CEN-CENELEC pages say no citation is expected. Not yet a legal duty: the portals are the national bodies' answer to a judgment on access to documents. The Commission's proposal for a new Standardisation Regulation would make free access a duty; it is a proposal and can change. t: Where ENISA consults: ten channels, two feeds, and drafts that are announced elsewhere
x: ENISA does not publish more than it did in 2023, but in more places and by more rules. Its certification work consults in an orderly way on its own website. Its guidance for manufacturers under the Cyber Resilience Act was put out for comment in 2026 as PDF files on its server, mostly without a news item on its site, and became known through LinkedIn and community mailing lists. The Cybersecurity Act 2 would make such guidance a standing task of ENISA, so far without a duty to consult on it.

t: Wo ENISA konsultiert: zehn Kanäle, zwei Feeds und Entwürfe, die anderswo angekündigt werden
x: ENISA veröffentlicht nicht mehr als 2023, aber an mehr Orten und nach mehr Regeln. Ihre Zertifizierung konsultiert geordnet auf einer eigenen Website. Ihre Leitfäden für Hersteller nach dem Cyber Resilience Act gingen 2026 als PDF-Dateien auf ihrem Server in die Konsultation, meist ohne Meldung auf ihrer Website, und wurden über LinkedIn und Mailinglisten der Community bekannt. Der Cybersecurity Act 2 würde solche Leitfäden zur Daueraufgabe der ENISA machen, bisher ohne Pflicht, dazu zu konsultieren.

t: ENISA ad hoc working group on 5G cybersecurity certification (EU5G) (ENISA AHWG 5G)
x: Tasks To enhance the framework on 5G cybersecurity and secure 5G deployment in the European Union, the European Commission requested ENISA (upon its mandate to develop cybersecurity certification schemes: Article 8 Cybersecurity Act) to develop a candidate European cybersecurity certification scheme for 5G networks (EU 5G scheme). Upon the task to prepare the candidate EU 5G cybersecurity certification scheme, ENISA launches this call for expression of interest for participation in an Ad Hoc Working Group (EU5G AHWG). What is the aim of the EU5G AHWG? This candidate EU 5G scheme addresses only a part of the 5G eco system that was selected by the Member States, based on criteria to achieve stakeholder value and manageable scheme development. Based on this approach, the project will focus on the following use cases for cybersecurity certification: The supply and deployment of identified 5G network equipment Management of subscriber identities Remote SIM provisioning 5G authentication (incl. roaming) Subscriber connectivity services Composition The DECISION No 73/2021 of ENISA's Executive Director of 25 October 2021 has established the ad-hoc group and the lists of selected candidates for membership. The decision was then amended by DECISION No 79/2021 and DECISION No 04/2022. Members appointed to the Ad hoc Working Group on the candidate EU 5G Cybersecurity Certification Scheme:

t: ENISA ad hoc working group on cloud services certification (EUCS) (ENISA AHWG Cloud Services)
x: Tasks In accordance with article 48(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/881 (hereinafter, Cybersecurity Act), ENISA seeks to assist the European Commission in the preparation of a candidate cybersecurity certification scheme on cloud services. Scope The scope of this cybersecurity certification scheme will address such aspects as, stimulating the uptake of cloud services among users, user trust to cloud services and the provision of cloud services by service providers; this scheme will further support data mobility as well as compliance with the EU legal framework on the digital single market. This scheme could be further developed to meet vertical sector requirements, as necessary and in line with EU policy. The scope of this ad hoc working group is to support ENISA in preparing the above-mentioned draft candidate cybersecurity certification scheme. Key tasks of this ad hoc working group include a review of existing cloud security certification schemes, a precise scoping of the future candidate scheme, the pre-qualification of elements that ENISA needs to include in a cybersecurity certification scheme, support the drafting of a scheme in line with the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2019/881 and generally support ENISA in carrying out its tasks in relation to the preparation of this draft candidate cybersecurity certification scheme.

Date Document Kind Subject Status Access Text 20 Nov 2026 A10-0314/2026 EP committee report Report on the proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on the safety, resilience and sustainability of space activities in the … Our summary: Report of Parliament's Industry, Research and Energy committee on the EU Space Act proposal, adopted in committee on 19 November 2026 and tabled for plenary on 20 November 2026; it is the committee's text for the plenary vote, not Parliament's position and not law. Like the rapporteur's draft report, it removes the proposal's own cybersecurity regime for space operators (risk management, incident reporting and the resilience annex) and instead extends the space sector of the NIS 2 Directive to all space activities, space services and Union-owned assets, with transposition 24 months after entry into force; unlike the draft, it keeps the link to NIS 2 as a without-prejudice clause and drops the reduced duty to report incidents. It also cuts the authorisation deadline to six months with tacit approval where national law allows (not for launch services), adds a security and defence filter for authorisations, exempts SMEs and research institutions from the environmental footprint rules and deletes the Union Space Label; none of the tracked concepts is touched. public – en 20 Nov 2026 WK 18038/26 Council note EU Space Act - Space-based data - activities - PowerPoint
